1.goal: To name the scene she already knows — a hotel desk — and to say once what today gives her: a way to ask for a repeat.
run: Ask what she does today when someone at a desk asks her something she does not understand.
Take the answer as it comes. Portuguese is fine here.
Say once what today is: she learns to ask people to say it again, and everybody does this, in every language.
exact: What today is: "Today you learn to ask people to say it again. Everybody does this — in every language."
If she says she just smiles and nods: "That works once. Today you get two sentences that work every time."
1.expected: Some version of pointing, smiling, or handing over the phone. That is the honest starting point, and it is the one the lesson replaces.
1.support: If nothing comes, offer two: does she point at things, or does she hand over her phone?
1.challenge: Ask her whether it has ever cost her something on a trip.
1.monitoring: Whether she describes a strategy or an avoidance. Both are useful; only one of them she can keep.
1.evidence: What she does today when she does not understand — the before of this lesson.
1.transition: Move on when she has told you how she manages today.

2.goal: To place the scene: the hotel from lesson 1, two people at the desk, three short questions.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the brief with her.
Confirm two things: there are three questions, they are short, and the answers are the sentences she already has from lesson 1.
Do not say what the three questions are. That is the next screen.
2.expected: She connects it to lesson 1: same hotel, same booking, and she already has the answers.
2.support: If she looks worried, point at the second sentence of the brief — the answers are hers already.
2.challenge: Ask which of her four sentences from lesson 1 she thinks will be useful here.
2.monitoring: Whether lesson 1 comes back on its own, or has to be pointed at.
2.evidence: Whether the four sentences of lesson 1 survived a week.
2.transition: Move on when she knows what she is about to hear.

3.goal: To have her guess the three questions before hearing any of them.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. Portuguese accepted.
run: Read the three questions on screen out loud with her, and ask for a guess on each.
Do not confirm and do not correct. These are hypotheses.
Accept Portuguese, and give the guess back in English so she hears it once.
exact: Giving a guess back in simple English: "So: your name, and how many nights. Say it with me — my name, and how many nights."
If nothing comes, the two options: "Your name and the dates, or your name and the price?"
3.expected: Name and nights usually come up. Breakfast usually does not.
3.support: Offer two options and let her choose. Choosing is still risking.
3.challenge: Ask which of the three has a number in the answer.
3.monitoring: Whether she guesses without being sure — this is the second lesson in which that matters more than the answer.
3.evidence: Whether guessing is getting easier than it was in lesson 1.
3.transition: Move on when she has guessed all three.

4.goal: To recognize WHICH question was asked — nothing more. No answers yet.
4.interaction: S listens; T controls the player.
run: The three questions are already on screen: she reads them before you play anything.
Play the three, one at a time, with a pause between them.
Do not open the transcript — it belongs to stage 5. And do not translate: say it in English, more slowly.
Use the Slower button rather than your own voice when she misses one.
4.expected: She identifies each question by what it asks for: the name, the nights, breakfast.
4.support: Play it again at Slower, and let her hear it a third time if she asks. Asking for a repeat is the content of this lesson — do not take it away from her here.
4.challenge: Ask how many people speak, and how she can tell.
4.monitoring: Whether she needs one, two or three listenings. It is the first isolated measure of her listening.
4.evidence: How many listenings each question needed, and whether she asked for the repeat herself.
4.transition: Move on when she has recognized the three.

5.goal: To connect each thing said at the desk with what it is asking for, now with the transcript available.
5.interaction: S classifies on screen, T checks with her.
run: She classifies the six lines. Check together.
Discuss only the ones she got wrong.
Two CCQs: how many people spoke? (Two.) Did anybody ask for her passport? (No.)
5.expected: Six classified. The two that trip people up are the spelling question and the line about breakfast times — neither is a question about her.
5.support: If she is stuck on a line, play just that line again before you explain anything.
5.challenge: Ask which of the six is not a question at all.
5.monitoring: Whether she separates what is being asked from what is merely being said.
5.evidence: Whether the transcript changes her answers, and by how much.
5.transition: Move on when the six are checked.

6.goal: For her to see, herself, what works when she does not understand.
6.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S discussion.
run: Four reactions on screen; she marks the two that keep the conversation going.
Then ask, in Portuguese if you need to: what happens after each one?
Let her name the difference before you do.
6.expected: In her own words: the two that ask for something keep the conversation going; smiling and saying she does not speak English end it — and then the desk resolves everything by gesture, which is what already happens on her trips.
6.support: If she cannot say it, act out both endings — one where you repeat, one where you switch to gestures — and ask which one she wants.
6.challenge: Ask which of the two she would use first, and why.
6.monitoring: Whether she sees asking as a move, or as an admission.
6.evidence: How she describes what asking for a repeat means. It is the belief this lesson exists to change.
6.transition: Move on when she has named the difference.

7.goal: To get the five sentences said out loud, many times, and to have her ask for a repeat at least once without being told to.
7.interaction: T asks, S answers, live. Rounds, then out of order.
run: You ask, she answers. Three questions, three answers. Then again, out of order.
ONCE, speak too fast on purpose. She has to ask you to repeat.
If she asks, say out loud that this was exactly what the lesson wanted.
This is the longest stage, and that is deliberate.
exact: The fast one, said at normal speed and run together: "AndhowmanynightswillyoubestayingwithusMsAparecida?"
When she asks for the repeat: "That. That is the lesson. You just did it."
If she freezes instead of asking, give the opening: "Sorry…"
7.expected: My name is… · Four nights. · Yes, please. / No, thank you. · Sorry, again please? · More slowly, please.
7.support: If she freezes instead of asking, give the first word of the repair sentence and wait.
7.challenge: Ask the three in a row without pausing, and let her sort them out.
7.monitoring: Whether the repair comes on its own, or only after you prompt it.
7.evidence: Whether she asked for a repeat without being told to, and how many rounds it took.
7.transition: Move on when she has asked for a repeat at least once, on her own.

8.goal: For her to hold the whole desk exchange live, with nothing on screen — and to repair once.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are at the desk; she has just arrived.
run: Close the transcript before you start.
The whole desk: you ask the three, she answers the three. Say one of them fast.
Do not correct during the role-play.
Write down what she says, as she says it. This is the first isolated measure of her listening, and it is what the next lesson is planned from.
exact: Opening the desk: "Good afternoon. Checking in?"
The three, one at a time: "What is your name, please?" / "And how many nights?" / "Would you like breakfast in the morning?"
If she answers with a gesture, ask for the sentence: "In a sentence, please."
8.expected: Three answers in sentences, and one repair when the fast question arrives.
8.support: If she answers with a gesture, ask again and wait for a sentence.
8.challenge: Add a fourth question she has the language for: "And your booking number?"
8.monitoring: Whether the answer comes as a sentence or as a gesture, and whether the repair holds under pressure.
8.evidence: The three answers as she said them, and whether the repair happened without a prompt.
8.transition: Move on when the three have been answered.

9.goal: To give back one thing, and then to run the same three questions a little faster with one repeat allowed.
9.interaction: T–S, then a replay with the player.
run: One thing, not two.
Then play the audio a little faster, with one repeat allowed. Count the repeats with her.
Say why it is counted: asking for a repeat is what this lesson measures, and it is the thing that changes a whole trip.
Do not add content here.
exact: Before the replay: "A little faster this time. You can stop me once — choose your moment."
9.expected: The three answered at the faster speed, with one repeat used deliberately.
9.support: If one repeat is not enough, allow a second and say so out loud. The number is not the point; using it is.
9.challenge: Run it with no repeat allowed and see what she does instead.
9.monitoring: Which question she spends her one repeat on.
9.evidence: Where she chose to spend the repeat — it tells you which of the three is hardest for her.
9.transition: Move on when the replay is done.

10.goal: To name what she did, and to announce the lesson she has been waiting for without knowing it.
10.interaction: T–S. She ticks what she recognizes; the confidence row is hers.
run: She marks what she recognizes on screen.
Say the homework out loud, and do not put it on screen: the post-class has the three questions at normal speed and two free resources.

Announce lesson 3 — the verb she herself named in the consultation, to be. Say that she has already used it four times in the first two lessons, and that next week it gets its name. That sentence matters: she said she got stuck because she did not know this verb.
Fill in the post-lesson record before you close.
exact: Announcing lesson 3: "You have already used this verb four times in two lessons. Next week we give it a name."
10.expected: Some of the items ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If she ticks nothing, read the list with her and ask which one she could use at a desk tomorrow.
10.challenge: Ask which of today's five sentences she would use first.
10.monitoring: Her reaction to the announcement about the verb. It is the sentence this whole block was built around.
10.evidence: Whether she asked for a repeat on her own during the lesson, and what she said when lesson 3 was announced.
